name: ccache
baseline: Uncached compilation (same compiler command run without ccache); the page does not involve Make/Ninja and does not name the compiler
workload: Median of 100 runs compiling ccache's own ccache.c (-g -O2 -MD) and a preprocessor-heavy c++_includes.cc (-MD), comparing no-cache vs ccache's direct/preprocessor/depend cache-hit modes.
claimed_speedup: ccache.c: 145.39x (direct mode), 137.81x (depend mode), 28.33x (preprocessor mode) vs no cache. c++_includes.cc: 29.10x (direct), 29.32x (depend), 5.09x (preprocessor) vs no cache.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not named on page; -g -O2 -MD plus needed -I flags (ccache.c); -MD only (c++_includes.cc); ccache 3.7.1
hardware: Intel Core i5-4690K, standard SSD, Linux desktop
stars_or_usage: 3.0k stars; bundled/used by default in many Linux distro and CI C/C++ build pipelines
tradeoffs: Only accelerates cache-hit rebuilds; provides no benefit on true cold/clean builds; requires stable compiler/flags/includes for hits; direct mode is disabled by some preprocessor macros (e.g. __TIME__).
caveats: Measures single-file cache hits against a plain uncached compile, not an end-to-end Make/Ninja build, so real speedup depends on hit rate. Cache misses are slower than no cache: first-time runs were 0.96-0.98x (ccache.c) and 0.83-0.97x (c++_includes.cc), and the page cites 5-20% miss overhead (1-3% in depend mode). The page does not name the compiler or give a date. It was measured with the old ccache 3.7.1 on a dated i5-4690K. ccache is itself a named baseline of the compile-caching-and-distribution category.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/ccache/ccache + WebFetch https://ccache.dev/performance.html

verification.tier_reason: First-party page lists the CPU (Core i5-4690K, SSD), flags (-g -O2 -MD / -MD), ccache 3.7.1 and median-of-100 method, and the repo has a timing script (misc/performance). But the page never names the compiler or its version, and it does not link the script, so this is not tier A. First-party numbers with partial methodology are tier C.
verification.notes: All six speedup factors match the page exactly. The downgrade is only because the compiler is unnamed; the rest of the methodology is solid. The GPL-3.0-or-later license is confirmed from LICENSE.adoc (gh shows NOASSERTION), and stars are 2,961.

name: tup
workload: Synthetic C project generator (logarithmic directory tree, up to 100,000 C files / ~200,000 total files with headers): cold build, single-file-change rebuild, and no-op ('nothing changed') dependency check, tup vs make.
claimed_speedup: At 100k files: no-op check ~0s (tup) vs ~30 minutes (make); single C-file change rebuild ~0.1s (tup) vs ~30 minutes (make). Cold/initial build: tup is 5-30% SLOWER than make across sizes.
tradeoffs: Requires all build outputs declared explicitly (no implicit globbing) for correctness; runs a persistent filesystem-watching 'monitor' process; much smaller ecosystem/IDE support than Make/CMake.
caveats: First-party page with no CPU model, OS or compiler flags stated, and the generator script is not published. The ratio (about 30 min vs 0.1 s) looks implausible, so it is capped at tier C under the >50x rule. The page footer shows a 2008-2024 copyright, so the hardware is likely old. At 100k files the log-scale graphs appear to put make at a little over 1,000 s (about 20 min), which is below the text's 'half an hour'. The near-zero no-op and update times rely on tup's file monitor, which took 9.7 s to start the first time at 200k files and 2 min 30 s with a cold cache (2.5 s hot). The 100k-file case is a stress test, and tup's cold build is 5-30% slower than make.

name: NativeLink
baseline: local, non-distributed single-machine build (no remote cache / no distributed compilation)
workload: Full LLVM + Clang project build (~4,468 build actions, culminating in llvm-readelf) via CMake+Ninja and the recc REAPI client, comparing a local laptop build to the same build distributed across a home Kubernetes/Talos cluster through NativeLink.
claimed_speedup: Independent blog (Reid Kleckner, 2026-03-30): a full LLVM + Clang build with CMake/Ninja took 1026.169s locally on the author's laptop (Ninja default -j, no remote execution, PCH disabled) vs 257.527s distributed through recc + NativeLink at -j96 over WiFi, about 4.0x (the intro says 'four times faster than my laptop, going from 1026s to 253s'). With PCH enabled, the local build took 682.778s, and the author writes that 'the distributed build is only 2.65x faster than the local build', calling the 4x an 'overstatement'. In the recc build directory, a clean rebuild with a full cache hit rate took 92.885s vs 266.600s for the preceding cold build (over VPN). NativeLink's homepage separately claims '4-15x faster builds' demonstrated on LLVM, with no methodology.
compiler_and_flags: Toolchain from LLVM's ghcr.io/llvm/ci-ubuntu-24.04 container (LTO/BOLT-optimized clang); CMake + Ninja with recc as the compiler launcher; the linked demo repo's reconfig.sh uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, LLVM_TARGETS_TO_BUILD=X86, CMAKE_DISABLE_PRECOMPILE_HEADERS=ON; distributed run at -j96, local run at Ninja's default -j
hardware: Client: the author's laptop (model and CPU not stated), over WiFi (the cache test was over a VPN). Remote: a home Kubernetes cluster on Talos Linux made of small, low-power control nodes plus extra unpictured nodes; the author says his Framework desktop 'is doing most of the heavy lifting'. No CPU models are stated.
stars_or_usage: 1.6k stars; vendor claims 10B+ build requests/month in production, used by Samsung and others
tradeoffs: Requires standing up a CAS/remote-execution server (Docker/Kubernetes) rather than a single local binary; core cache is source-available FSL-1.1 (converts to Apache-2.0 two years after each release) and some modules (metrics, persistent-worker) are Business Source License requiring a commercial license for shared production use; integrates via the Bazel Remote Execution API (Bazel, Buck2, reclient/recc, etc.) rather than being a drop-in ccache/distcc substitute.
caveats: Single-author personal experiment, one run per configuration, by an independent LLVM/Clang contributor. It compares a laptop against a laptop plus a remote cluster (mostly a Framework desktop), not against distcc, icecc or ccache. The author concedes the 4x headline is an overstatement: with PCH enabled locally the gain is 2.65x, because recc could not handle PCH. No CPU models are given. NativeLink's '4-15x' homepage figure has no published methodology. License is FSL-1.1-Apache-2.0 (not OSI; each release converts to Apache-2.0 after two years).
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/TraceMachina/nativelink (direct lookup of a known Bazel-REAPI-compatible remote cache/execution project); benchmark surfaced via repos/TraceMachina/nativelink/contents/llms-small.txt and its linked post https://reidkleckner.dev/posts/llvm-recc-nativelink/

The 'LLVM builds 4 times faster ... 17 minutes to 4' vendor quote was not found; the homepage says '4-15x faster builds'. name: Intel oneAPI DPC++/C++ Compiler (icpx)
workload: Runtime of a single-threaded equity-volatility quant pipeline (parse ~30M option quotes from a 1 GB pcap, Black-Scholes implied-vol Newton inversion, SVI smile fits, greeks) built with GCC, Clang and icpx from identical source in strict-IEEE and fast-math variants.
claimed_speedup: icpx-fast finishes the pipeline 1.79x faster than gcc-strict (13700 ms vs 24536 ms total, single-threaded, median of 7 reps). The README text says 1.44x faster than the best non-Intel variant (clang-fast-zmm, 20453 ms), but its own table gives 1.49x (derived from page data); against gcc-fast (21554 ms) it is 1.57x (derived from page data). Under strict IEEE the field compresses to 1.00-1.23x (icpx-strict 19920 ms vs gcc-strict 24536 ms vs clang-strict 22475 ms). Stage detail for icpx-fast vs gcc-strict: SVI fit 2385 ms vs 8879 ms (3.7x) and greeks 770 ms vs 2571 ms (3.3x); on the Newton IV stage gcc-fast is faster (3.07 vs 2.83 Mq/s).

name: LLVM lld (LLVM linker)

Docs text: 'you can expect that LLD runs more than twice as fast as the GNU gold linker' on a large program on a multicore machine.
hardware: Independent run: AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX 16-core/32-thread, 92 GiB RAM, output on tmpfs. lld docs table: 2-socket 20-core 40-thread Xeon E5-2680 2.80 GHz with an SSD drive

caveats: The lld docs table is first-party, undated but from about 2017 (the same page says 'as of February 2017'; the file was rewritten to Markdown on 2026-07-16 without changing the table); the four programs, link command lines, compiler and flags are not given. name: RapidProto
workload: Decoding a realistic 2000-record mixed Dataset payload (strings, nested/repeated messages, packed scalar arrays) serialized by protoc, plus protobuf's own google_message1/google_message2 corpora and a 20MB OpenStreetMap PBF extract
claimed_speedup: ~7x faster arena decode than protoc+google::protobuf::Arena (g++-13; ~6x on clang++-20), with ~0.49x peak payload memory; streaming decoder ~12x faster than protoc+Arena and ~1.8x faster than protozero; +61% MB/s vs protoc on the OSM PBF protobuf-layer decode

C++, gcc 11.3.0, Protobuf 3.21.12 vs Zserio 2.10, on an Intel i7-9850H under Linux Mint 21.1.
claimed_speedup: Zserio-generated C++ decodes faster than protoc-generated C++ (ParseFromString) on all 4 datasets: addressbook 1.478ms vs 1.731ms (~1.17x), apollo 0.244ms vs 0.641ms (~2.63x), carsales 1.374ms vs 2.053ms (~1.49x), simpletrace 0.221ms vs 0.386ms (~1.75x).
